munikids10:
Before "indie golf" was a hashtag, Muni Kids was already in the trenches. Brothers Maxton and Drew Reinland started the brand in Portland in 2015 with a simple premise: make gear for the people who learned the game on public courses, not the ones with legacy memberships. Eleven years later, they've built an entire world around that idea — headcovers, apparel, art, a podcast, urban golf meetups, a children's book called Golforia, and a brick-and-mortar shop inside Portland's Memory Den.

This is the brand that proved muni golf had a culture before anyone thought to monetize it. The price range sits at $30 to $85, the aesthetic leans screen-printed and hand-drawn, and the whole operation still feels like it's run by two guys who'd rather be walking nine holes than taking a meeting. If you've been looking for the origin story of this whole movement, it starts here.
hats14:
The hat game in indie golf right now is absurd in the best way. Fourteen picks, fourteen brands, and not a single logo you'd find in a corporate pro shop. We pulled from art-driven studios, small-batch makers, and the kind of labels that treat a rope cap like a canvas.

Radry's mid-crown number splits the difference between dad hat and structured cap with Tony Knapton's hand-drawn graphics doing all the talking. From there it fans out — brands that treat headwear like their flagship product, not an afterthought. Price range sits between $35 and $65, which means you can grab two or three without losing sleep. If your hat rotation is still all tour logos and freebies from demo days, this is the reset.
manorsgj:
Manors teamed up with Gentleman Jack to do something that sounds like a stretch on paper but lands perfectly on the hanger. The entire capsule pulls its paisley print from engraved detailing on vintage Gentleman Jack bottles, and the fabric story is just as considered — Seawool made from recycled oyster shells and plastic bottles, UV 50+ protection, four-way stretch throughout.

The range runs $21 to $283, covering everything from course-ready pieces to the kind of lifestyle gear that plays equally well at a whiskey tasting or a Saturday morning tee time. Manors keeps proving they can do collabs without diluting their identity, and this one might be their most interesting yet. Whiskey branding on golf apparel shouldn't work. It does.
malbongallo:
Malbon's summer drop channels the Gallo Colorido — Portugal's iconic painted rooster — and the whole collection carries that Mediterranean warmth. Lightweight nylon-spandex windshirts, partial zips, high collars, and a color palette that runs through Chive, Surf Spray, and Cream. Every piece says coastal resort without the try-hard energy.

The construction is built for the reality of summer golf: transitional conditions, marine layers that burn off mid-round, and mornings that start cool and end sticky. Prices run $45 to $168, keeping it accessible for a brand that often pushes higher. This is Malbon doing what they do best — taking a cultural reference point and making it feel natural on the first tee.
specialday:
Every golfer in Austin has their regular muni rotation, but sometimes you need something bigger. A birthday round. An anniversary. A Tuesday where you just need to feel like you're on vacation. This is the list for that — eight courses within driving distance of Austin that justify the splurge and the extra hour in the car.

Wolfdancer Golf Club out in Lost Pines leads the pack — Arthur Hills carved it through the property like he had personal beef with flat terrain, and the closing stretch from 14 to 18 is one of the best in Texas. Fazio Canyons at Barton Creek, Ram Rock at Horseshoe Bay, and the underrated Vaaler Creek in Blanco round out the top. Green fees run from $52 at Falconhead to $275 at Barton Creek, so there's something here whether you're treating yourself or going all in.
hoodies14:
Fourteen hoodies from twelve brands, and every single one was designed by people who actually play golf. This isn't the fleece wall at your local sporting goods store. It's the intersection of streetwear weight, course-ready cuts, and the kind of graphics that make you look like you know something the rest of the foursome doesn't.

Eastside Golf's Core Fleece Swingman sets the tone at ~$88 — premium cotton, Swingman embroidery, streetwear DNA. From there, Gumtree Golf goes heavyweight at $145, Malbon pushes into the $185 range with the Safety Buckets Fesque, and Casualist keeps it understated at ~$85. Brands like Sounder, Sugarloaf Social Club, and Jones Golf Bags fill the middle. Whether you need a layer for early morning tee times or a post-round pullover that doesn't scream "I just played 18," the edit covers it.
golfbooks7:
Seven books. No gimmicks. These are the ones that keep showing up on the nightstands of golfers who actually get better — the titles your teaching pro has read twice and your playing partner quotes on the back nine without realizing it.

Ben Hogan's Five Lessons is the foundation. Harvey Penick's Little Red Book is the soul. Rotella's Golf is Not a Game of Perfect rewires your mental game, and Zen Golf by Dr. Joseph Parent takes it deeper. Pelz's Short Game Bible is the technical manual for everyone losing strokes inside 100 yards. Nilsson and Marriott's Every Shot Must Have a Purpose connects the dots between practice and play. All under $17 each. The cheapest equipment upgrade you'll ever make.
putters26:
The 2026 putter market is stacked. Eight new flatsticks from eight different makers, and the technology gap between the big names and the boutique shops has never been smaller. L.A.B. Golf's LINK.2.1 brings Lie Angle Balance to a traditional blade at $599. Scotty Cameron's Phantom 5 and Bettinardi's BB1 hold the heritage lane. Toulon Design's Austin H1 — yes, named after our city — sits at $600.

Mizuno's M.Craft City Series at $350 is the value play. Swag Golf's Handsome One at $400 is the culture play. Evnroll's ER2 Origin and LA Golf's Bel-Air X round out a lineup where every option has a real argument behind it. If you've been rolling with the same putter since 2019, this is the year that changes.
radrygolf:
Tony Knapton runs Radry Golf out of Sheboygan, Wisconsin, and the brand is exactly what happens when an artist decides golf gear is his medium. Every hat, crewneck, and headcover starts as one of Tony's illustrations — hand-drawn, art-school energy, zero corporate polish. The smiley-face logo is becoming one of the most recognizable marks in independent golf, and the brand's gallery arm through White Dot Market sells signed prints alongside $42 dad hats.

The lineup runs from Custodian Hats and Dive Team caps at $42 up through the Contrast Quarter Zip at $120, with the Bugging Blade Cover ($65) and Smoke Em' Ashtray ($55) filling in the weird-in-a-good-way accessories lane. Collabs with Seamus add credibility, but Radry doesn't need borrowed clout. This is a brand that treats golf like a canvas, and the canvas keeps getting bigger.
accessories:
Six accessories from six different brands, and none of them came from a pro shop impulse rack. This is the edit for golfers who care about the small stuff — the brush clipped to your bag, the headcover protecting your putter, the water bottle that actually looks good sitting in your cup holder.

Dimple & Divot's Murphy Hickory Brush ($45) is handcrafted in Raleigh with American hickory and nylon bristles. Sentinel Golf's Basecamp Water Bottle ($68) is titanium and built to last longer than your swing changes. Depeche Golf contributes Issue #4 of their print magazine, Mogshade brings a Portuguese-made headcover, Walker Golf adds a ball marker three-pack, and Jones rounds it out with the Ranger Cooler. Different countries, different categories, same idea: the details matter.
munigrub:
Austin has five public golf courses and the on-course food situation at each one tells a very different story. We ranked every food spot across the muni system — from vending machines to full-service cantinas — so you know exactly what you're walking into before you tee it up.

Fairways Cantina at Morris Williams takes the crown. Cisco's Muny Cafe at Lions Municipal is a close second — the kind of no-frills counter that's been fueling rounds since before most of us were born. Stag & Finch at Jimmy Clay/Roy Kizer holds down third, and Hancock's clubhouse window rounds out the list with vending-machine vibes redeemed by the neighborhood restaurants nearby. If you're choosing your muni based on the course alone, you're only getting half the picture.
merrillgolf:
Merrill Golf calls itself a design venture through the lens of golf, and that's not marketing language — it's a literal description of how the brand operates. No polos. No moisture-wicking polyester. Instead: acid-washed tees, heavyweight hoodies, five-panel caps, and a flying-duck logo that channels vintage Americana more than any country club.

The Target Practice Tee ($60) and Golf Company Tee ($55) are the entry points — graphic-heavy, built on premium blanks, designed to be worn as much off the course as on it. The Birds Dad Hat ($50) and Target Practice Zip Hoodie ($150) round out a tight catalog that feels more tackle shop than fairway. Merrill is making golf apparel for people who fish, hunt, and happen to play golf — and it turns out that audience is bigger than anyone expected.
golfbags:
Seven bags from six brands, and every one of them was designed by people who think your bag should look as considered as the rest of your kit. This is not a roundup of whatever's on sale at the big-box stores. This is the short list for golfers who treat their bag like the centerpiece it is.

Jones leads with the 2026 Trouper 4.0 ($315) and the Heritage Trouper ($375) — two different takes on the same obsessive design philosophy. MacKenzie's 8-inch Waxed Canvas Mac ($740) is the heirloom play. Vessel's Lux Stand ($399), Stitch's SL2 Gen 2 ($398), and Shapland's Kantle 3.1 ($490) hold the premium middle. Ghost Golf's Anyday Kovert Ops ($415) rounds it out with a tactical edge. These are the bags people notice on the first tee.
metalwoodss26:
Metalwood Studio's SS26 collection is ten pieces deep and every single one looks like it was designed by someone who grew up on skate graphics and indie zines. The Double Plaid Windbreaker ($288) is the headliner — full patchwork in a relaxed cut that's loud enough for the first tee and light enough for the bar after. The adidas x Metalwood MC70 Golf Shoe ($200) anchors the footwear side of the collab.

In between, the King of the Greens Jersey ($168) and Micro Grid Button Up ($168) handle the technical-but-stylish lane, while the Digital Hombre Top and Short ($154/$136) push the pattern work into new territory. Hats at $48 and $58 keep the entry point accessible. Metalwood keeps doing what nobody else in golf is willing to try, and SS26 might be their most confident collection yet.
sentinel1733:
Sentinel Golf linked up with Chicago bag maker 1733 on a capsule built around Saltex — a triple-layer Japanese nylon that's salt-bath heat-treated for a dense, organic texture you won't find anywhere else in golf. The material is the story: rigid out of the box, softens with humidity, snaps back when it dries. DWR coated throughout.

The lineup covers a shoe bag ($138), tote ($320), and duffle ($320), all in Saltex Charcoal. Sentinel also dropped the V4 Bag Brush in Olive ($128) alongside the collab pieces. Everything is made in Chicago, everything is limited, and the material process alone justifies the price tags. Two brands that obsess over craft, working in a fabric that most golf brands wouldn't even know how to source.
casualist:
Casualist and Walker Golf share this double feature, and together they paint a picture of where indie golf apparel is headed — elevated basics, earthy palettes, and the kind of restraint that lets the fabric do the talking. Casualist's side runs from the All The Gear Sweatshirt ($140) and Cart Path Ripstop Jacket ($339) down to a $21 ball marker, covering polos, trousers, tees, and caps in muted tones that look good against any course backdrop.

Walker Golf fills the second half with Australian-rooted pieces — the Jersey Knit Sweater, Kookaburra Quilted Vest, and a Walker x adidas Ultimate365 Jacquard Polo at $100. Both brands share a philosophy: make things that work on the course and still look right at the pub after. No neon. No logos you can read from the fairway. Just good clothes for golfers who've outgrown the pro shop.
premtees:
Six golf tees. All of them cost more than the fast-food lunch you grabbed on the way to the course. And somehow, every one of them makes a case for why the upgrade is real.

Flightpath's Diamond Tee ($23 for eight) is polycarbonate, diamond-shaped, and packaged in a matchbox — the aerodynamics pitch actually holds up under testing. Bird Darts went bamboo at $6.99 for 18. Western Birch hand-paints striped birch tees. Lignum machines micro-sized wooden tees in Germany. Green Swing does sustainable bamboo. And Brimz Supply made cigarette-shaped tees called Tee Box Smokes ($12.99 for 10), which is either genius or unhinged depending on your sense of humor. The humble golf tee got interesting when nobody was looking.
boldtees:
Twelve graphic tees from eleven brands, and every one of them says something about who you are on the course without requiring a conversation. This is the roundup for golfers who want their shirts to have a point of view — not a swoosh and a tagline, but actual design intent.

Quiet Golf's Monogram Washed Pocket Tee ($55) leads with tonal subtlety. Random Golf Club's S.F.E. Clubhouse Tee ($40) and Students Golf's Grass Obsession ($52) bring the community energy. Devereux, Manors, Radry, Metalwood Studio, and GGNC fill the middle with graphics that range from cactus art to medieval crests. Kingfisher Golf's Getting Worse Tee ($34.99) is the most honest shirt in the game. Walker Golf and Merrill Golf close it out. Prices run $34.99 to $62 — low enough to stock up, high enough that the blanks are actually good.
19thhole:
The round is over. The sun is dropping. You're sunburned, slightly dehydrated, and not ready to go home. Austin has you covered.

Five spots, five different vibes, all designed for the golfer who treats the 19th hole like the most important one. Equipment Room at Hotel Magdalena on Music Lane brings the craft-cocktail-and-vinyl energy. Only The Wild Ones on South Congress is the patio hang. Frazier's Long & Low on the South Shore keeps it low-key. Domo Alley-Gato on East 6th is the outdoor bar with games and tacos. And The Golden Horn on North Loop is the neighborhood spot where nobody cares that you're still wearing golf shoes. No reservations needed, no dress code enforced, no judgment for ordering a second round before 6 PM.
threeputtround:
European brand 3 Putt Round has one joke and they commit to it completely: golf is an addiction, so the accessories should look like vices. Tees come packaged in cigarette boxes and matchbooks. The branding leans hard into punchy colors, cheeky copy, and the kind of packaging that belongs on a shelf as much as in your bag.

The lineup runs from Golf Tee Matches at 20 euros to the Addiction Knitted Polo at 120 euros, with towels, caps, and various tee packs filling in the middle. The Vecchio x Lost Balls Towel collab adds some crossover credibility. Everything ships from Europe, everything is designed to make your playing partners do a double take when you pull tees out of what looks like a pack of smokes. It's novelty done with enough craft and humor that it actually sticks.
